channel.title: Captain Dadders — Flight Expeditions
channel.description: Following the Lewis & Clark Corps of Discovery route by air — MSFS 2024 expedition blog.

item.title: Leg 35: Beaver Bark and Buffalo Wool — NA45 to 4NA0
item.description: Sixty-six miles northwest up a reservoir-wide Missouri from the Four Bears Peninsula to a hard-to-find airstrip near Watford City. On the river below in April 1805, the Corps found the best beaver of the whole trip, buffalo too lean to eat, two days of wind, and Assiniboine sign everywhere without a single Assiniboine.

item.title: Leg 34: The Great Bend and the White Bear — 37N to NA45
item.description: Eighty miles northwest over Lake Sakakawea from Garrison Dam to Sandstrom Airstrip on the Four Bears Peninsula. On the river below in April 1805, the Corps rounded the Great Bend, nearly lost a loaded pirogue twice, reached the mouth of the Little Missouri, and found the first grizzly tracks.

item.title: Leg 33: In Honour of Our Neighbours — Y19 to 37N
item.description: A long-delayed return to the cockpit retraces the ground where Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1804-1805 at Fort Mandan, met Sacagawea and Charbonneau, and set out again in spring.

item.title: Leg 32: The Cannonball and the Slant Village — Y27 to Y19
item.description: An evening flight north from Standing Rock past Bismarck to a grass landing at Mandan, with the Corps of Discovery's last Arikara contact, a river-stone anchor hauled aboard at the mouth of the Cannonball, the Corps' first grizzly encounter, and the abandoned Mandan town of On-a-Slant just below the leg's landing point.

item.title: Leg 31: Headwind to Standing Rock — KMBG to Y27
item.description: Forty-nine nautical miles north up Lake Oahe from Mobridge to Standing Rock Airport, past the drowned mouth of the Grand River, with the Corps of Discovery's four-day council at the Arikara villages, an Arikara chief boarding the keelboat for a peace mission to the Mandans, John Newman's court-martial, and the expedition's first camp in present-day North Dakota.

item.title: Leg 30: Across Lake Oahe — KPIR to KMBG
item.description: An hour up Lake Oahe from Pierre Regional to Mobridge Municipal, with the Corps of Discovery's escape from the Lakota at the Bad River, the meeting with trader Jean Vallé at the Cheyenne, and the first grizzly tracks at the Moreau.

item.title: Leg 29: The Teton Standoff — 9V9 to KPIR
item.description: An evening flight up Lake Francis Case to Big Bend Dam, around the Big Bend of the Missouri, and on to Pierre, SD — where in 1804 the Corps of Discovery faced down the Teton Sioux in the most dangerous diplomatic encounter of the outbound year.

item.title: Leg 28: Starved in a Land of Plenty — 2SD2 to 9V9
item.description: Over the drowned Missouri — Lake Francis Case — to a hard crosswind landing at Chamberlain, while in 1804 the Corps finds Shannon starved among the buffalo, takes its first pronghorn, and counts 3,000 bison at one view.

item.title: Leg 27: Old Baldy and the Prairie Dog Town — Y03 to 2SD2
item.description: A run up the Missouri across the Nebraska–South Dakota line — the Niobrara confluence, Old Baldy, and Fort Randall Dam — paired with the Corps of Discovery's arrival on the open plains, the first prairie dog town, and Clark's '500 Buffalow,' September 3 to 9, 1804.

item.title: Leg 26: The River Becomes a Lake — KYKN to Y03
item.description: A short hop over Gavins Point Dam and Lewis and Clark Lake — the moment the wild Missouri becomes a reservoir — paired with the Corps of Discovery's first council with the Yankton Sioux at Calumet Bluff, August 28 to September 2, 1804.

item.title: Leg 25: A Side Trip to Spirit Mound — KVMR to KYKN
item.description: Captain Dadders re-creates the August 25, 1804 Spirit Mound side trip by air, then contrasts the captains' nine-mile cross-country slog in 86° heat with the modern 1.4-mile trail — and reflects on what has been lost from the landscape they surveyed from the summit.

item.title: Leg 24: Into Bison Country — KSUX to KVMR
item.description: A sunset hop from Sioux City up to Vermillion past the Missouri/Big Sioux confluence — paired with four days of Corps history: a new sergeant elected, the first buffalo, a burning bluff, and a hill of 'little devils' just over the horizon.

item.title: Leg 23: Hallowed Ground — KTQE to KSUX
item.description: A long, straightened-river run from Tekamah up to Sioux City: searching for Blackbird Hill, a windy landing beside Sergeant Bluff, and the story of pelicans, an empty Omaha village, the end of the deserter chase, and the death of Sergeant Floyd — the expedition’s only loss.

item.title: Leg 22: The First Council — KOMA to KTQE
item.description: A short 72 NM hop from Omaha up to Tekamah, Nebraska, with a detour over the site of Lewis & Clark's first formal council with Native Americans near Fort Atkinson — where the speeches landed less than the air gun, and where the Missouri River has since wandered three miles east of the bluff.

item.title: Leg 21: The Great River Platte — MO24 to KOMA
item.description: An evening flight up the Missouri to Omaha, reaching the mouth of the Great Platte and landing at Eppley Airfield — on the very ground where Lewis & Clark camped on July 27, 1804.

item.title: Leg 20: A Fevered River, and a Promise in Washington — 64MO to MO24
item.description: A short, calm hop past St. Joseph from Booze Island to Lonesome Sky — while back in 1804, Lewis & Clark fought a sickly, fevered week on the river and President Jefferson welcomed the Osage to Washington.

item.title: Leg 19: The First Fourth — KMKC to 64MO
item.description: A 39-minute hop from Kansas City's downtown airport to Booze Island, threading past Fort Leavenworth and Lewis and Clark Lake — and overflying Independence Creek, where on July 4, 1804, the Corps fired the swivel gun at sunrise, named the creek for the occasion, and shared out an extra gill of whiskey: the first Independence Day celebration west of the Mississippi.

item.title: Leg 18: A Fine Place for a Fort — 71MO to KMKC
item.description: A perfect-weather sunrise flight up a peaceful, farm-quilted Missouri — land that was once an ocean of tallgrass prairie — to a downtown landing at Kansas City's Charles B. Wheeler Airport. In June 1804 the Corps of Discovery camped three days at Kaw Point, where the Kansas River meets the Missouri: they threw up a log redoubt against the Kansa (then, as Clark wrote, "out in the plains hunting the Buffalow"), the captains judged a rise up the river "a butifull place for a fort," the hunters caught the expedition's first sight of buffalo, and two privates drew the lash for raiding the whiskey barrel before the boats pushed on. The fine place for a fort would not become Kansas City for another half-century.

item.title: Leg 17: An Eventful Passage — KJEF to 71MO
item.description: An eventful afternoon up the Missouri from Jefferson City to a building-less grass strip near Wakenda — fair skies giving way to rain and thunderstorms, past Boonville (named for Daniel Boone’s salt-making sons, and unsettled in 1804), and a wind-tossed approach before a lonely landing at Famuliner Farms. It was along this same bend, on June 4, 1804, that the Corps of Discovery broke the mast of their keelboat beneath a leaning sycamore — the very mishap the Lewis & Clark monument on the Jefferson City capitol grounds quietly commemorates — before fighting past Arrow Rock, taking on the old interpreter Pierre Dorion, and making new rope and oars at Rope Walk Camp while mosquitoes, dysentery, and Clark’s stubborn cold wore on the party.

item.title: Leg 16: The River of the Osage — MU68 to KJEF
item.description: A quick 25-minute hop up the Missouri from the Gasconade River, past an unnoticed Chamois, to just beyond the mouth of the Osage River — landing at Jefferson City Memorial Airport. The Osage gave its name to the Wahzhazhe, a powerful nation the Corps of Discovery had heard described as large, well proportioned, and very warlike, yet had not met: three weeks up the Missouri, their only contact with Native peoples had been friendly and fleeting. The free-flowing Osage of 1804 is today impounded behind Bagnell and Truman dams as the Lake of the Ozarks and Truman Reservoir. The same stretch that took 25 minutes by air cost Lewis and Clark six days against the current.

item.title: Leg 15: Beyond the Last Village — 1H0 to MU68
item.description: An early-morning launch up the Missouri to beat incoming weather, rewarded with sunrise over the river. Past Washington, Missouri — the Spanish-era "St. John Meyer's Settlement," newly American in 1804, with Daniel Boone settled across the river — and the site of La Charette, the last white settlement the Corps of Discovery would see before the Pacific. It was near here, at the cliffs above Tavern Cave, that Meriwether Lewis nearly fell to his death on May 23, 1804, saving himself with his knife. A satisfying grass-strip landing at Eu-Wish Airport near the Gasconade River.

item.title: Leg 14: The Third River — KCPS to 1H0
item.description: Up the Mississippi past an industrial-looking St. Louis and the Gateway Arch to the confluence with the Missouri — where the Corps of Discovery wintered on the Illinois side — then a left turn onto the third river of the trip. Just past St. Charles to Creve Coeur Airport (1H0), close to where the expedition was 222 years ago to the day: Clark and the crew had finally started up the Missouri on May 14, 1804, with Clark in command while Lewis stayed in St. Louis arranging an Osage chiefs delegation to Washington. A gusty crosswind made for a grass-then-pavement landing.

item.title: Leg 13: At the Gateway — 6MO2 to KCPS
item.description: Up the Mississippi from Ste. Genevieve, past the limestone quarry bluffs that gave the Ste. Genevieve Limestone formation its name, and north toward St. Louis — where the Corps of Discovery spent the winter of 1803–1804 at Camp Dubois on the Illinois side, waiting for the Louisiana Territory to officially transfer to the United States. A Gateway Arch flyby before landing at St. Louis Downtown Airport (KCPS) in Cahokia, the site of the historic Cahokia Courthouse that Lewis used as his winter headquarters.

item.title: Leg 12: The Vanished Capital — 12LL to 6MO2
item.description: Up the Mississippi past the vanished first capital of Illinois — Kaskaskia, stranded west of the river by the great flood of 1881 — and Fort Kaskaskia, where the Corps of Discovery recruited a dozen men and the captains split for the first time, before landing on the Ste. Genevieve Flying Club grass strip in Missouri.

item.title: Leg 11: Past Cape Girardeau — KCIR to 12LL
item.description: Continuing up the Mississippi from Cairo with the good fortune of a tailwind — exactly where Lewis and Clark's hard upstream pull began. Many river islands and rain clouds in the distance, past Cape Girardeau, Missouri (population ~40,000 today; only a handful of settlers in 1803, when it was a Spanish-administered trading post run by Commandant Louis Lorimier from his famous Red House), to a bouncy landing on a small grass strip next to a farm at Lambdins Field in Wolf Lake, Illinois.

item.title: Leg 10: Reaching the Mississippi — M30 to KCIR
item.description: A short evening hop from Metropolis to Cairo, Illinois — where the Ohio River ends and the Mississippi begins. The confluence at Cairo evokes Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn as much as Lewis and Clark, and a dramatic near-stall landing at Cairo Regional caps off a brief but eventful leg.

item.title: Leg 9: Past Diamond Island — KEHR to M30
item.description: Back to the skies after a family-visit layover in Henderson, Kentucky — a flyover of Diamond Island (an Ohio River pirates' hideout and a Lewis & Clark campsite on November 5, 1803), past the mouth of the Wabash where Indiana gives way to Illinois, and a reflection on the Ohio as the boundary between slave Kentucky and the free territory to the north in 1803, before landing at Metropolis, Illinois near historic Fort Massac.

item.title: Leg 8: Into the Setting Sun — KY8 to KEHR
item.description: A calm evening departure from Lewis Field in Lewisport, Kentucky, heading west into a setting sun over the river islands — Ellis Island and the French Islands — before passing Owensboro and Evansville and landing at Henderson City-County Airport, a town that, unlike its neighbors, was already six years old when Lewis and Clark floated past in 1803.

item.title: Leg 7: Below the Falls — KJVY to KY8
item.description: Departing Clark Regional and heading downstream past Louisville and Clarksville — the same stretch the full Corps of Discovery first traveled together in October 1803 — past a remarkable corridor of power plants, around the Horseshoe Bend of the Ohio near Leavenworth, Indiana, and past the Cannelton Hydroelectric Plant before landing at Hancock County Airport / Lewis Field in Lewisport, Kentucky.

item.title: Leg 6: Clark's Country — 4KT4 to KJVY
item.description: A peaceful cruise down the Ohio past the Milton-Madison Bridge and the massive Clifty Creek power plant, landing at Clark Regional Airport in Clark County, Indiana — the county and airport bearing the name of William Clark's older brother George Rogers Clark, the Revolutionary War hero who secured the Northwest Territory and founded Clarksville just downstream.

item.title: Leg 5: Queen City to the Fossil Lick — KLUK to 4KT4
item.description: Flying past downtown Cincinnati — the Great American Ballpark, the Bengals' stadium, and the skyline — then following the Ohio River southwest into Kentucky, landing at Steele's Bottom near Warsaw, close to Big Bone Lick, where Lewis collected mastodon fossils for President Jefferson before departing on the expedition.

item.title: Leg 4: River Highway to Cincinnati — I41 to KLUK
item.description: Past West Virginia at last, with Kentucky on the left and Ohio on the right. The Ohio River in 1803 was a bustling highway of westward migration — settlers, merchants, traders, and Native peoples all sharing the corridor. Towns lined the banks just as they do today, and the river barges are still going strong.

item.title: Leg 3: Above the Morning Fog — 75D to I41
item.description: The river valley was draped in mist with hilltops emerging above the clouds — exactly the kind of scenery Lewis would have seen pushing downriver in the autumn of 1803.

item.title: Leg 2: Wheeling and the Mound — 1G8 to 75D
item.description: Following the Ohio River south from Toronto, Ohio through the industrial river towns of Steubenville and Wheeling, West Virginia — passing the remarkable Grave Creek Mound, the largest surviving Adena burial mound in the United States, before landing at New Martinsville.

item.title: Leg 1: Departing Pittsburgh — 31D to 1G8
item.description: Lifting off from Inter County Airport in Irwin, Pennsylvania and following Meriwether Lewis's exact 1803 route down the Ohio River — past the Point where three rivers meet, over the historic Weirton/Steubenville corridor, and landing at Toronto, Ohio.
